question:
You are a researcher studying causal relationships using Blicket experiments. In these experiments, certain objects (called 'blickets') have the hidden property of activating a detector, causing its light to turn on.

Each example shows the results of placing different combinations of objects on the detector. Each object is described by color, material and shape. Your task is to determine whether a new combination of objects will cause the detector to activate.

After observing the previous examples, respond with:
- "on" if you can determine the detector light will turn on
- "off" if you can determine the detector light will stay off
- "undetermined" if there is insufficient evidence to reach a conclusion

Do not use quotation marks in your answer.

Previous experimental results:
green rubber sphere → off
brown metal sphere, green rubber sphere → on
brown metal sphere → on
yellow rubber cylinder, red metal cylinder → on
blue metal sphere, cyan rubber sphere → off
blue metal sphere, cyan rubber sphere → off

New test case:
yellow rubber cylinder

What is the detector light status?

IMPORTANT: When you finish, put ONLY the final answer inside \boxed{...} (no extra text). If the task requests a multi-line format, encode it into a single line representation.

[1] Detecting blickets: how young children use information about novel causal powers in categorization and induction - PubMed
    URL: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11108092/
    Published: 2016-06-01T00:00:00.000Z
    Author: A Gopnik 1 , D M Sobel
    SUMMARY: The study titled "Detecting blickets: how young children use information about novel causal powers in categorization and induction" investigates how children categorize objects based on their perceived causal properties. In the experiment, a "blicket detector" was used, which activated when specific objects were placed on it. The children observed that an object labeled as a "blicket" triggered the machine. The research specifically examines how children, aged 2 to 4 years, categorize objects like a "green rubber sphere," "brown metal sphere," and "yellow rubber cylinder" based on their causal powers, revealing insights into their cognitive development and understanding of causality. This experiment highlights the role of novel causal information in children's learning and categorization processes.
    HIGHLIGHTS:
      - Three studies explored whether and when children could categorize objects on the basis of a novel underlying causal power. To test this we constructed a "blicket detector," a machine that lit up and played music when certain objects were placed on it. First, 2-, 3- and 4-year-old children saw that an object labeled as a "blicket" would set off the machine. In a categorization task, other objects were demonstrated on the machine. Some set it off and some did not. Children were asked to say which ...
      - object on the basis of the associated event. Young children also sometimes made interesting memory errors-they incorrectly reported that objects with the same perceptual features had had the same causal power. These studies demonstrate that even very young children will easily and swiftly learn about a new causal power of an object and spontaneously use that information in classifying and naming the object.

    SUMMARY: The article "The Blicket Within: Preschoolers’ Inferences About Insides and Causes" investigates how preschoolers infer causal properties based on the internal parts of objects. It describes four experiments focusing on 4-year-olds' understanding of the relationship between an object's internal components and its causal abilities. 

In the context of your query regarding the "green rubber sphere," "brown metal sphere," and "yellow rubber cylinder," the experiments demonstrate that children can recognize that objects with different internal parts have distinct causal properties. For instance, when presented with objects, children were able to infer that if an internal part from one object was transferred to another, the causal properties would also transfer. This suggests that preschoolers can make inferences about causality without needing explicit labels or prior knowledge about the objects.

    URL: https://cocosci.princeton.edu/tom/papers/bayesblicket.pdf
    Published: 2011-03-16T00:00:00.000Z
    Author: Tom Griffiths
    SUMMARY: The paper "Bayes and Blickets: Effects of Knowledge on Causal Induction in Children and Adults" explores how individuals, including children and adults, infer causal relationships from limited observations using Bayesian inference. It investigates how prior knowledge about causal mechanisms influences these inferences, particularly in tasks involving objects like "green rubber spheres," "brown metal spheres," and "yellow rubber cylinders." The authors conducted five studies to analyze how variations in prior probabilities and the nature of causal relations (deterministic vs. probabilistic) affect judgments about these objects in a blicket detector context. Results indicated that adults' judgments aligned closely with Bayesian predictions, while children's responses qualitatively supported the model, suggesting that both groups utilize prior knowledge and statistical evidence in causal reasoning. This research highlights the interplay between learned knowledge and observed data in understanding causal structures.
